title: Response trajectory spectrogram — field journal
body:
Goal:
This note captures an exploratory profiling pass across a week of production traces with the intent to: 1) characterize p50/p95/p99 shapes for a set of workload cohorts, 2) produce a ‘spectrogram’ style view of per-stage timing across emission position (token index), and 3) surface hypotheses for the prominent long-tail modes we observed.

Why a spectrogram?
Traditional waterfall snapshots are good for single traces but miss the time-varying signature across token positions and cohorts. A lightweight spectrogram (heatmap of median/p95/p99 per-stage vs token index) helps spot modes that only appear after N tokens, or that correlate with KV-miss events or batching transitions.

Data sources and selection:
- Window: 2026-02-22 -> 2026-02-28 (peak weekday traffic + one deploy)
- Sampling: stratified trace sample from our SLO-driven sampler (weights: route traffic volume * route error margin). Kept both streaming and non-streaming responses.
- Cohorts: short (<= 64 input tokens), medium (65–256), long (>256). Also separate cold-start traces (GPU context load < 200ms before request).
- Representative trace IDs (for follow-up replay): trace-a1f3b2, trace-b4c9d8, trace-c8e7f1, trace-d12a90 (listed in linked Jira).

Summary observations (top-level):
- p50 is dominated by token compute (attention + matmul kernels) as expected. Typical p50 end-to-end: short 22ms, medium 48ms, long 110ms.
- p95 shows a second mode: queueing + batch formation latency spikes that align with mid-sequence emission boundaries (we see bursts where batch formation waits for 8ms windows).
- p99 reveals at least three distinct phenomena: KV-cache cold misses (heavy penalty), transient GPU context contention (interleaved high tail on adjacent workloads), and an egress backpressure step when emit stage batches exceed a small threshold (we saw sharp increases at >32 token emissions in flight).

Per-stage breakdown (median / p95 / p99) — aggregated numbers (ms):
(Stages abbreviated: TOK=tokenize, SCH=scheduler enqueue+wait, KV=kv lookup/hit/miss, CMP=attention+compute, EMIT=emit/pack, EGR=egress/net)

Short cohort (<=64):
- TOK: 0.6 / 1.8 / 3.5
- SCH: 1.2 / 6.5 / 18.0
- KV: 1.0 / 2.0 / 22.5
- CMP: 12.5 / 18.3 / 60.1
- EMIT: 4.3 / 10.1 / 28.8
- EGR: 2.4 / 4.6 / 9.0
- End-to-end (median/p95/p99): 22 / 43 / 120

Medium cohort (65–256):
- TOK: 0.7 / 2.0 / 4.0
- SCH: 2.1 / 9.0 / 32.0
- KV: 1.3 / 3.5 / 35.2
- CMP: 38.9 / 75.6 / 210.4
- EMIT: 6.0 / 15.2 / 64.0
- EGR: 2.8 / 5.5 / 11.7
- End-to-end: 48 / 155 / 410

Long cohort (>256):
- TOK: 0.9 / 2.6 / 5.2
- SCH: 3.9 / 14.4 / 56.2
- KV: 2.1 / 6.4 / 88.7
- CMP: 82.5 / 220.4 / 840.3
- EMIT: 9.3 / 27.0 / 180.5
- EGR: 3.4 / 7.0 / 17.9
- End-to-end: 110 / 540 / 1,200+

Notable patterns in the spectrogram slices:
- Token-index dependency: CMP p95/p99 climbs superlinearly after token index ~80 for long cohort. That aligns with attention kernel switching (small -> large window) and also with increased KV misses for streamed prefixes.
- Periodic microburst spikes every ~16 tokens in SCH stage: these match the async-batcher handoff boundary when the batcher flush interval aligns with incoming request phase shifts.
- Emit-stage quantization steps: EMIT p95 seems to jump on multiples of ~8ms, suggesting our emit aggregator flush granularity or serialization path has discrete commit/flush steps.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) KV-cache cold paths (evictions + async fetch) are a dominant contributor to p99 for medium/long sequences. Evidence: traces with high p99 often show a 40–200ms KV penalty correlated with recent model-switch events or after node restarts.
2) Batcher flush alignment creates a cohort of requests that wait for the flush window and then all contend for GPU kernels causing compute tail. Evidence: spectrogram gaps lined up with batcher flush intervals; p95 increases when effective batch size > 8.
3) GPU locality and multi-tenant warping: when adjacent workloads run kernels with differing register pressure we get context switching overheads visible as 100–300ms spikes in CMP.
4) Egress/emit backpressure: when concurrency of streaming clients crosses threshold, serialization in emit path causes step function in latency.

Immediate mitigations to validate (short experiment list):
- Experiment A: force synchronous KV warmup for top-1k routes (preheat KV entries at request start) for 48h; measure p99 delta.
- Experiment B: change batcher flush policy from 8ms fixed-window to adaptive (wake-on-first-request + max-window 12ms) for a small subset of nodes. Compare p95.
- Experiment C: add per-kernel run tagging in traces to correlate kernel type with p99 spikes (low effort: add kernel-id to span metadata).
- Experiment D: increase emit pipeline parallelism (allow two concurrent emit flusher threads) behind a feature flag for high-throughput routes.

Instrumentation gaps / asks:
- Current traces do not capture per-token kernel timings reliably (we get stage-level but not kernel-level). Request: add optional high-fidelity token-level timestamps (sampling at 1 in 100 traces).
- KV cache diagnostic: we need per-request KV eviction markers (evict/repopulate) and size-at-lookup to identify cold vs stale misses.
- Batcher internals: expose flush-window alignment timestamp in trace so we can correlate waiting time with flush boundaries.

Open questions / to be answered in follow-ups:
- Are kv-miss heavy traces correlated with specific model versions or with autoscaler events? (early signal: higher after model switchover)
- How much of the long CMP tail is due to sequence-length-driven kernel choice rather than contention? Need controlled replay of sequences on isolated nodes.
- Does the emit-serialization step exist in all languages/clients or only the streaming path?

Next steps (owner: Samir / Priya):
- Samir: spin up a 48h controlled experiment for Experiment A (KV warmup) on canary traffic; instrument metrics and capture full traces. Target start: 2026-03-15.
- Priya: prototype adaptive batcher policy in branch runtime/batcher/adaptive-flush and attach kernel-id tagging to traces. PR link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/842.
- Ava: prepare a short dashboard (Grafana) showing spectrogram heatmap by cohort, and add quick links to representative traces in the dashboard.

Notes to self (rough):
- When replaying traces, be sure to replay with same model-variant + quantization profile; we saw different kernels pick for Q4 vs Q8 which confounds comparison.
- Save raw p99 traces separately — they’re useful for kernel post-mortem.

Appendix — quick trace snippets (human-readable):
trace-a1f3b2 (medium) — timeline:
0.0ms TOK
1.8ms SCH wait (6.2ms wait due to flush)
8.2ms KV hit
12.1ms CMP start -> 66.5ms (gradual tail, kernel-switch at token 90)
66.6ms EMIT -> 82.4ms EGR finish

trace-c8e7f1 (long, p99) — KV cold miss observed (120ms) and CMP contention (320ms spike)

If you want, I can:
- 1) produce the Grafana spectrogram panels and attach screenshots, or
- 2) run a small single-node replay harness for the top 10 p99 traces and summarize kernel-level timings.

Comments welcome — feel free to add inline trace IDs you want me to prioritize for replay.
